outro: Adapted from The Roots of Capitalism, by Prabir Purkayastha, from Tricontinental.

parts.title: Sugar built capitalism
parts.hook: The first global commodity wasn't oil. It was sugar.

beats.label: England
beats.say: In {1226|twelve twenty-six}, England's King Henry the Third was ready to pay roughly 450 US dollars, in today's money, for three pounds of sugar.

beats.label: West Africa → Caribbean
beats.say: Sugar travelled with a second commodity: enslaved Africans, captured in Africa and sold in the Caribbean and the Americas.

beats.label: Caribbean plantations
beats.say: On the plantation, enslaved people grew the cane, crushed it and boiled it, on one site. Field and factory in one.

beats.label: Colonies vs. England
beats.say: Investments in the sugar colonies were four to seven times more profitable than investments in England.

beats.label: British imports, 1774
beats.say: By {1774|seventeen seventy-four}, raw sugar made up one fifth of all British imports, more than any other good.

parts.title: The plantation's journey
parts.hook: The slave plantation wasn't invented in the Americas.

beats.label: The Black Death
beats.say: Between {1347|thirteen forty-seven} and {1351|thirteen fifty-one}, the Black Death drastically reduced the supply of peasant labour around the Mediterranean.

beats.label: Sicily · Cyprus · Rhodes · Crete
beats.say: So the rulers of Sicily, Cyprus, Rhodes and Crete imported enslaved people from North Africa to work the sugar.

beats.label: Merchant capital
beats.say: Merchant families from Venice and Genoa invested in these plantations. Here, merchant capital and modern slavery were married.

beats.label: Gulf of Guinea
beats.say: Portugal took the model to São Tomé: land from the king, capital from Venice or Genoa, enslaved people from Africa.

beats.label: Then the Caribbean
beats.say: The Portuguese carried the São Tomé model to Brazil. From there, it spread to the Caribbean, and later to North America.

parts.title: Replaceable by design
parts.hook: Planters found it cheaper to replace people than to keep them alive.

beats.label: Holes dug per day
beats.say: At planting time, each worker in the first gang had to dig sixty to one hundred holes by hand, every day.

beats.label: Harvest shifts
beats.say: During the harvest, enslaved people worked eighteen to twenty hour shifts in the mills and boiling houses, six days a week.

beats.label: Barbados
beats.say: A Barbados planter, Edward Littleton, estimated that a sugar estate would kill all one hundred of its enslaved workers in nineteen years.

beats.label: Dead within a year
beats.say: By one contemporary estimate, two in five newly arrived enslaved people died within their first year.

beats.label: Owners in Britain
beats.say: Owners, often far away in Britain, tracked their return on investment in account books, much like today's spreadsheets.

parts.title: The human toll
parts.hook: At least ten million people landed. The real number seized was far higher.

beats.label: Landed in the Americas
beats.say: At least ten million enslaved Africans are estimated to have landed in the Americas and the Caribbean.

beats.label: Total seized
beats.say: Counting deaths during capture, marches, detention and the Middle Passage, the total seized was plausibly fourteen to twenty million.

beats.label: On British ships, 1640–1807
beats.say: Between {1640|sixteen forty} and {1807|eighteen oh seven}, British ships forced about 3.1 million Africans across the Atlantic. Around 2.7 million survived.

beats.label: Muskets per person
beats.say: Early in the {1700s|seventeen hundreds}, one enslaved person was exchanged for two muskets. By the end of the century, at least fifteen.

beats.label: Population growth
beats.say: From the seventeenth to the nineteenth century, Asia and Europe grew by 300 percent or more. Africa stayed almost the same, and fell in many regions.

parts.title: Britain's sugar factories
parts.hook: Before the textile mills, some of Britain's earliest factories refined slave-grown sugar.

beats.label: Britain's refineries
beats.say: Refineries spread from Plymouth to Glasgow and London to Liverpool, burning coal under large copper pans.

beats.label: Sugar imports, 1700–1800
beats.say: Between {1700|seventeen hundred} and {1800|eighteen hundred}, British sugar imports grew sevenfold, to about 152,000 tonnes.

beats.label: Jamaica's sugar exports
beats.say: Between {1682|sixteen eighty-two} and {1701|seventeen oh one}, Britain took more than 95 percent of Jamaica's sugar exports.

beats.label: Britain, 1770
beats.say: One estimate: in {1770|seventeen seventy}, close to 40 percent of the capital for Britain's commercial and industrial expansion came from slave trade profits.

beats.label: Tariff on Indian sugar
beats.say: After conquering India, Britain added an extra 25 percent tariff, protecting its refiners and plantations from Indian sugar.

parts.title: Sugar, silver and money
parts.hook: The global financial system grew out of sugar, silver and slavery.

beats.label: The asiento
beats.say: In {1513|fifteen thirteen}, the Spanish Crown issued the first asiento: a licence to sell enslaved Africans to its colonies.

beats.label: World silver, 1494–1850
beats.say: Between {1494|fourteen ninety-four} and {1850|eighteen fifty}, Spanish America, mostly Potosí and Mexico, supplied 80 percent of the world's silver.

beats.label: Acapulco → Manila
beats.say: Minted into the Spanish silver dollar, it sailed from Acapulco to Manila, and was accepted for trade across Asia, the Americas and much of Europe.

beats.label: Amsterdam → London
beats.say: Control of sugar and the trade in enslaved people helped make the Dutch guilder, then the British pound, the reserve currency of its era.

beats.label: Still with us
beats.say: The configuration of power behind modern capitalism dates back at least around five hundred years.
